title: Output-Space Allocation Costs for Calibration-Guided LLM Compression: An Empirical Study

contributions.purpose: Test whether aligning ROCKET's global MCKP allocation cost with its output-space factorization objective improves compressed model fidelity.
contributions.mechanism: ROCKET-ActCost, which replaces ROCKET's weight-space Frobenius allocation cost in the multi-choice knapsack problem with an output-space equivalent computed from matrices already available during profiling.
contributions.evaluation: On Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8 percentage points higher average accuracy across 8 zero-shot benchmarks (53.1% vs 52.3%).
contributions.source_quote: An empirical study of output-space MCKP allocation cost for calibration-guided LLM compression, testing whether aligning the allocation objective with the factorization objective improves model fidelity.

contributions.purpose: Characterize the downstream effects of switching the allocation objective.
contributions.mechanism: Joint measurement of zero-shot task accuracy and WikiText language modeling perplexity under aggressive compression with output-space vs weight-space costs.
contributions.evaluation: Accuracy-perplexity tradeoff on Qwen3-8B at 50% compression: task accuracy improves (+0.8pp) but WikiText perplexity worsens by 16% (61.46 vs 52.98); on Llama-3.2-1B at 20% compression both metrics improve, suggesting the tradeoff is setting-dependent.
contributions.source_quote: Discovery of an accuracy-perplexity tradeoff: output-space cost improves task accuracy but worsens language modeling perplexity under aggressive compression.

contributions.purpose: Explain why the allocation-cost change produces only a modest effect.
contributions.mechanism: Correlation analysis between weight-space and output-space per-layer errors and the resulting divergence in MCKP allocations.
contributions.evaluation: Error correlation exceeds 0.99, with only 70 of 252 layers receiving different allocations, fundamentally limiting allocation divergence and explaining the modest effect size.
contributions.source_quote: Analysis showing that high error correlation (>0.99) between weight-space and output-space metrics fundamentally limits allocation divergence, explaining the modest effect size.

self_declared_provenance.quote: ROCKET (Ali et al., 2026) is a recent training-free compression method that combines sparse-dictionary factorization with global budget allocation via a multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP). ... However, when allocating compression budgets across layers, ROCKET uses weight-space Frobenius error as the MCKP cost rather than the output-space error that motivated the factorization.

Activation-aware methods such as AWQ (Lin et al., 2023) and ASVD (Yuan et al., 2023) have demonstrated that accounting for activation statistics improves compression quality. We hypothesize that using output-space error as the MCKP allocation cost—which directly measures the impact of compression on layer outputs for the calibration distribution—may yield better downstream performance than weight-space error.

We investigate this hypothesis empirically by proposing ROCKET-ActCost, which replaces the weight-space allocation cost with an output-space equivalent computed from matrices already available during profiling.

notes: Self-labeled 'empirical study' with mixed/modest results: small accuracy gain traded against 16% perplexity degradation, and the paper itself explains why the effect is small (>0.99 error correlation). No separate related-work section on pages 1-2 (page 2 goes directly to Method); provenance quotes are all from the introduction. All three contributions are framed as study/finding rather than a headline new method, though ROCKET-ActCost is a concrete method variant of ROCKET (Ali et al., 2026).
